That's not a fixed test with better sensitivity; it's barely a test at all. The responsible fix is to keep alpha at a level that reflects the real cost of a false positive for this deployment (commonly 0.05, sometimes lower for higher-stakes decisions) and, if power against a real, meaningful effect size is genuinely too low at that alpha, increase the sample size instead -- the one lever that raises power without also inflating the false-positive rate.

assessments.prompt: In a hypothesis test comparing a new model's latency to an old model's, which scenario describes a Type II error?
options: The test rejects H0 even though the two models truly have identical average latency.
The test fails to reject H0, even though the new model truly does have a different average latency.
The test correctly fails to reject H0 because the two models truly have identical average latency.
The test correctly rejects H0 because the new model truly does have a different average latency.
assessments.explanation: A Type II error is a false negative: H1 is actually true (a real difference exists) but the test fails to reject H0 anyway. Option A describes a Type I error (a false positive), the opposite mistake. Options C and D both describe correct decisions, not errors -- C is a true negative, D is a true positive (power).

assessments.prompt: Holding the true effect size and alpha both fixed, which change increases a test's statistical power?
options: Increasing the sample size in each group.
Increasing the standard deviation (noise) of the underlying measurements.
Decreasing the sample size in each group.
Switching to a stricter (smaller) alpha, with nothing else changed.
assessments.explanation: More data tightens the sampling distribution of the test statistic under H1, reducing its overlap with the null distribution and increasing the chance a real effect is detected -- exactly what this concept's simulation showed, with power climbing from 0.175 at n=20 to 0.985 at n=300. Option B is wrong because more noise widens the sampling distribution and reduces power. Option C is the reverse of the correct lever. Option D is wrong because a smaller alpha shrinks the rejection region, which reduces power (as this concept's alpha sweep shows directly), not increases it.

assessments.prompt: A team lowers their significance threshold from alpha=0.05 to alpha=0.01 for model-comparison tests, keeping sample size and the true effect fixed, specifically to reduce false positives. What happens to beta (the Type II error rate) as a direct result, all else equal?
options: Beta decreases as well, since a stricter test is better along every dimension.
Beta increases, because shrinking the rejection region makes it harder for a real, fixed-size effect to be detected with the same amount of data.
Beta is unaffected, since it depends only on sample size, not on alpha.
Beta becomes exactly equal to the new alpha value, 0.01.
assessments.explanation: This is the alpha/beta tradeoff in action: for a fixed sample size and true effect, a smaller alpha shrinks the rejection region, which necessarily makes a real effect's test statistic less likely to clear the (now farther-out) threshold, raising beta. Option A ignores that this tradeoff exists at all. Option C is false -- this concept's alpha sweep, with n fixed, shows power (and therefore beta) changing substantially as alpha changes. Option D invents a numerical coincidence with no basis; alpha and beta are related by the tradeoff but are not generally equal to each other.

assessments.prompt: A safety-critical model deployment pipeline and a fast-iterating product experimentation team choose very different values of alpha for their hypothesis tests. Explain, in terms of the real costs of Type I vs. Type II errors, why that difference makes sense, rather than both teams simply using the conventional alpha=0.05.
assessments.modelAnswer:
Alpha and beta aren't abstract statistical settings -- they encode how costly a false positive (Type I error) is relative to a false negative (Type II error) in a specific real decision, and that cost ratio genuinely differs across contexts. In a safety-critical pipeline, wrongly concluding a new model is better and deploying it (a Type I error) can mean shipping something no safer, or actively worse, in a setting where mistakes are expensive, slow to detect, or hard to reverse. That team reasonably chooses a very low alpha (0.01 or smaller), accepting more Type II error risk -- a genuinely better model sitting unshipped a little longer while more evidence accumulates -- because the cost of a false 'ship it' verdict there is severe, and a delayed rollout of a real improvement is comparatively cheap.

A fast-iterating product team evaluating a button color or ranking tweak faces the opposite cost balance: a wrong 'ship it' call is cheap to detect through ongoing monitoring and trivial to revert, while a Type II error -- missing a real, if modest, improvement -- directly slows the team's overall rate of real improvement. That team can reasonably tolerate a higher alpha (0.10 or more), buying higher power against modest true effects in exchange for accepting more false positives, because false positives are cheap there and false negatives are the more expensive mistake.

Neither team is being statistically sloppy by deviating from 0.05 -- 0.05 is a convention, not a law -- they're each setting the threshold where it actually reflects what a wrong decision costs them.

concepts.title: p-Values and Critical Value Thresholds
concepts.description: A p-value is the probability, computed under the assumption that H0 is true, of seeing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed -- not the probability H0 is true, and not the probability of a false positive -- and it is mathematically just another way of asking whether the observed statistic falls inside the rejection region.
learningObjectives: State the precise definition of a p-value as a conditional probability computed under the assumption that H0 is true.
Explain, with a concrete reason, why a p-value is NOT the probability that H0 is true, and NOT the probability of a Type I error for this specific result.
Demonstrate the mathematical equivalence between 'p < alpha' and 'the test statistic falls inside the rejection region defined by alpha.'
Compute a one-sided and two-sided p-value from a test statistic and its null distribution using scipy.stats.
Identify common real-world sentences that misstate what a p-value means, and correct them.

sections.heading: The Precise Definition, Clause by Clause
sections.body:
A **p-value** is the probability, computed under the assumption that H0 is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed in your sample. Every clause in that sentence is load-bearing, and skipping any one of them is exactly how the definition gets misquoted.

'Computed under the assumption that H0 is true' means the p-value is a **conditional probability** -- conditioned on a specific model of the world (the null), not on your actual data being correct, not on any belief about which hypothesis is really true. It answers the question 'if H0 really held, how often would data like this arise from sampling noise alone?', not the reversed question 'given this data, how likely is it that H0 holds?' -- a distinction covered in full in the next section, and one of the most consequential mix-ups in applied statistics.

'At least as extreme' depends entirely on sidedness. For a two-sided test, 'extreme' means far from the null value in *either* direction, so the p-value adds up both tails; for a one-sided test, it means far in one specific direction only, so the p-value comes from a single tail.

```python
from scipy import stats

t_statistic = 2.87
df = 18

# Two-sided p-value: probability of a statistic at least this extreme,
# in EITHER direction, assuming H0 is true
p_two_sided = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t_statistic), df)

# One-sided p-value: probability of a statistic this large or larger,
# in ONE specific direction (H1: the true value is greater than H0's)
p_one_sided = stats.t.sf(t_statistic, df)

print(f"two-sided: {p_two_sided:.4f}")   # 0.0102
print(f"one-sided: {p_one_sided:.4f}")   # 0.0051 -- exactly half
```

`stats.t.sf` (the survival function, 1 - cdf) is used here rather than `1 - stats.t.cdf(...)` purely for numerical precision -- for very extreme statistics, `cdf` can round all the way to 1.0 in floating point, silently zeroing out a p-value that should be a tiny but nonzero number, while `sf` computes the tail probability directly and keeps that precision. A smaller p-value always means the observed data would be rarer under H0 -- more surprising, in the specific technical sense this whole framework is built around -- and therefore stronger evidence against H0, exactly mirroring 'further into the rejection region' from the test-statistic framing of the previous concepts.

sections.heading: What a p-Value Is Absolutely Not
sections.body:
The single most consequential statistical misconception in applied work, without a close second, is treating a p-value as the probability that H0 is true (or, equivalently, as one minus the probability that the observed effect is 'real'). It is neither of those things, and the reason is a specific, nameable logical error: confusing a conditional probability with its reverse.

A p-value is P(data this extreme | H0 true). What people often want, and mistakenly believe a p-value gives them, is P(H0 true | data this extreme). These are, in general, completely different numbers, and conflating them is the exact same error as confusing 'the probability a test comes back positive, given that someone truly has a rare disease' with 'the probability someone truly has a rare disease, given that their test came back positive' -- the second one depends heavily on how rare the disease is in the first place (its base rate), information a p-value never has any access to, because a p-value's calculation never involves a prior probability that H0 is true at all. Computing P(H0 true | data) honestly requires Bayes' theorem and an actual prior probability for H0 -- a fundamentally different, Bayesian calculation that classical, frequentist hypothesis testing (the entire framework this module covers) simply does not perform.

A p-value is also **not** the probability that this specific test result is a Type I error. Alpha is a long-run property of the *testing procedure*, describing what fraction of the time a procedure like this one would produce a false positive *if it were run over and over on genuinely H0-true data* -- it is not a statement about the one dataset actually in front of you, which either does or does not represent a real effect, full stop, even though you can never know for certain which. And, echoing the previous concept's misconception, a p-value is **not** a measure of effect size or practical importance -- a minuscule, practically meaningless true difference can produce a vanishingly small p-value given enough data, exactly as a huge test statistic can, since a p-value is a direct, monotonic transform of the test statistic.

sections.heading: p < alpha Is the Same Decision as 'Statistic in the Rejection Region'
sections.body:
The p-value approach and the rejection-region approach from earlier in this module are not two competing methods that might occasionally disagree -- they are the exact same underlying comparison, expressed in two different but mathematically equivalent vocabularies. A p-value is a strictly decreasing function of how extreme the observed test statistic is (given a fixed null distribution and fixed sidedness): the more extreme the statistic, the smaller the p-value. That single fact is enough to guarantee p < alpha holds *exactly* when the test statistic falls inside the rejection region defined by that same alpha -- neither statement can be true without the other.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
mismatches = 0
n_checks = 1500

for alpha in [0.10, 0.05, 0.01]:
    for _ in range(500):
        a = rng.normal(0, 1, size=15)
        b = rng.normal(0.3, 1, size=15)
        t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(b, a)
        dfree = len(a) + len(b) - 2
        critical_value = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha / 2, dfree)

        decision_by_p = p_value < alpha
        decision_by_statistic = abs(t_stat) > critical_value
        if decision_by_p != decision_by_statistic:
            mismatches += 1

print(mismatches, "mismatches out of", n_checks)   # 0 mismatches out of 1500
```

Zero mismatches across 1500 independently generated datasets and three different alpha values is not a coincidental result of this particular simulation -- it's a mathematical certainty, and the code is really just a demonstration, not a test of something that could have come out otherwise. In practice, nearly everyone reports and reasons about p-values rather than raw critical values, because a p-value carries strictly more information: it tells you not just whether you'd reject at your chosen alpha, but the exact boundary alpha at which the decision would flip, letting a reader apply their own significance threshold to the same reported number.

sections.heading: Where p-Values Go Wrong in ML Practice
sections.body:
In applied ML work, p-value misuse tends to follow a predictable pattern: a comparison between model A and model B produces p = 0.03, and that single number gets treated as a final, settled verdict -- 'model B is better, case closed' -- with no accompanying effect size, no confidence interval, no mention of how much data went into that estimate, and no acknowledgment that a p-value alone says nothing about how large or reliable the apparent improvement actually is. A responsible report always pairs a p-value with the actual estimated difference (in accuracy points, latency milliseconds, conversion rate, whatever the metric is) and, ideally, a confidence interval around that estimate -- the p-value answers 'is this probably not just noise,' the effect size and interval answer 'how big, and how precisely do we know that.'

An even more consequential failure mode shows up specifically when many comparisons get made against the same validation set over the course of an iterative ML project -- trying twenty hyperparameter configurations, or a dozen feature-engineering variants, and checking each one's p-value against the baseline. Even if every individual test is computed correctly, running many of them and reporting only the smallest p-value you found (or treating any config that happened to clear p < 0.05 as a confirmed win) reintroduces exactly the kind of chance-driven false positive this whole framework was built to guard against -- just spread across many tests instead of one. That specific failure mode, and the corrections built to guard against it, is the entire subject of the next and final concept in this module.

examples.title: Computing a p-Value Two Equivalent Ways
examples.code:
from scipy import stats

t_statistic = 2.87
df = 18

p_via_cdf = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_statistic), df))
p_via_sf = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t_statistic), df)

print(f"{p_via_cdf:.4f}")   # 0.0102
print(f"{p_via_sf:.4f}")    # 0.0102 -- same answer, more numerically stable
examples.explanation: Both formulas compute the identical two-sided p-value, 0.0102, because `stats.t.sf(x, df)` is defined to equal `1 - stats.t.cdf(x, df)` exactly, just computed with a numerically more stable method for the far right tail. For a moderate statistic like 2.87 the two approaches agree to four decimal places, as shown here; the practical reason to prefer `sf` shows up specifically for very extreme statistics, where `1 - cdf(...)` can lose all its precision to floating-point rounding (cdf rounding to exactly 1.0) while `sf` keeps computing the true, tiny tail probability directly.

examples.title: The p-Value Decision Matches the Rejection-Region Decision, on Real Data
examples.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

old_latencies = np.array([118, 122, 115, 130, 121, 119, 125, 117, 123, 120])
new_latencies = np.array([110, 108, 115, 112, 109, 111, 107, 114, 110, 113])

alpha = 0.05
t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(old_latencies, new_latencies, equal_var=False)

var1, var2 = old_latencies.var(ddof=1), new_latencies.var(ddof=1)
n1, n2 = len(old_latencies), len(new_latencies)
df = (var1 / n1 + var2 / n2) ** 2 / (
    (var1 / n1) ** 2 / (n1 - 1) + (var2 / n2) ** 2 / (n2 - 1)
)
critical_value = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha / 2, df)

print(f"t_stat={t_stat:.3f}, critical_value={critical_value:.3f}, p_value={p_value:.2e}")
print("via p-value:          ", "Reject H0" if p_value < alpha else "Fail to reject H0")
print("via rejection region: ", "Reject H0" if abs(t_stat) > critical_value else "Fail to reject H0")
# t_stat=6.333, critical_value=2.134, p_value=1.44e-05
# both approaches: Reject H0
examples.explanation: This is the same latency dataset used in the previous concept's worked example, now checked both ways side by side. t_stat=6.333 clears the critical value of 2.134, and independently, p_value=1.44e-05 clears below alpha=0.05 -- both routes land on 'Reject H0' for the exact same underlying reason, because they are, mechanically, the same comparison. Reporting the p-value (1.44e-05) rather than just 'Reject H0' additionally tells a reader this result would still reject at a much stricter alpha, like 0.001 -- information the raw reject/fail-to-reject verdict alone doesn't carry.

examples.title: A p-Value Misinterpretation Checklist
examples.code:
p_value = 0.03   # result of comparing model B against model A

statements = [
    ("There is a 3% chance H0 (no real difference) is actually true.", False),
    ("If model A and model B truly performed identically, data producing "
     "a difference at least this large would occur about 3% of the time "
     "from sampling noise alone.", True),
    ("There is a 97% chance model B is genuinely better than model A.", False),
    ("This result has a 3% chance of being a Type I error.", False),
    ("The observed data would be fairly unusual under the assumption "
     "that there's no real difference between the models.", True),
]

for statement, is_correct in statements:
    verdict = "CORRECT" if is_correct else "WRONG (common misreading)"
    print(f"[{verdict}] {statement}")
examples.explanation: Running through a checklist like this against every p-value you're about to report is a cheap, mechanical habit that catches the vast majority of real-world misinterpretations before they reach a slide deck or a paper. The two CORRECT statements both keep the conditioning direction straight -- 'if H0 were true, this data would be unusual' -- while every WRONG statement quietly flips that direction into a claim about the probability of H0 itself, or of a Type I error specifically on this result, neither of which a p-value computes.

misconceptions.description: A p-value of 0.03 means there's a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true (or equivalently, a 97% chance the observed effect is real).
misconceptions.clarification: A p-value is P(data this extreme | H0 true), not P(H0 true | data) -- confusing the two is the same logical error as confusing a disease test's known accuracy with the actual chance someone has the disease given a positive result, which also depends on how common the disease is beforehand. Getting from a p-value to an actual probability that H0 is true requires Bayes' theorem and a prior probability for H0, a fundamentally different, Bayesian calculation that a classical p-value never performs.

misconceptions.description: A p-value tells you the probability that this specific significant result is a false positive (a Type I error).
misconceptions.clarification: Alpha is a long-run property of the testing procedure -- what fraction of the time a procedure like this one would produce a false positive if it were run repeatedly on genuinely H0-true data -- not a probability attached to this one dataset. This specific dataset either does or does not reflect a real effect, and no single p-value can tell you which, or attach a probability to which, on its own.

A p-value is P(data this extreme | H0 true) -- a probability computed assuming H0 is already true -- not P(H0 true | data). Computing the latter would require a prior probability for H0 and Bayes' theorem, which this code never uses.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The function simply relabels p_value as probability_h0_true and formats it as a percentage, producing a fluent-sounding but incorrect sentence. p=0.03 genuinely means: if the two models truly had identical average latency, data producing a gap this large or larger would occur about 3% of the time from sampling noise alone. It says nothing directly about the probability that the models truly have the same latency -- that would be P(H0 true | data), the reverse conditional, which is a fundamentally different quantity that a frequentist p-value calculation never computes and cannot be recovered from a p-value alone without an assumed prior probability for H0.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to compute a two-sided p-value from a t-statistic, but it's returning the wrong number and, in this specific case, the wrong conclusion. Find the bug and fix it.
exercises.code:
from scipy import stats

def two_sided_p_value(t_statistic, df):
    # Intended to compute a two-sided p-value
    return stats.t.sf(abs(t_statistic), df)

p = two_sided_p_value(t_statistic=1.9, df=18)
print(f"{p:.4f}")
print("Reject H0" if p < 0.05 else "Fail to reject H0")
hints: stats.t.sf(x, df) returns the probability in ONE tail only -- is that the full two-sided p-value, or just half of it?
Recall the earlier example in this concept: the two-sided p-value was computed as `2 * stats.t.sf(...)`, not `stats.t.sf(...)` alone.
Compute both the one-tailed value and its double for t=1.9, df=18 -- do they fall on the same side of the 0.05 threshold?
exercises.solutionExplanation: `stats.t.sf(abs(t_statistic), df)` returns only the probability in the single upper tail beyond abs(t_statistic) -- exactly half of the true two-sided p-value, which must add the symmetric lower tail too, hence the missing `2 *`. For t=1.9 and df=18, the one-tailed value is about 0.0368 (which happens to be just under 0.05), while the correct two-sided value is about 0.0736 (just over 0.05) -- the missing factor of 2 actually flips the printed conclusion from 'Reject H0' to the correct 'Fail to reject H0,' even though the underlying data and test statistic never changed. This is exactly the kind of silent, no-error-thrown bug that's dangerous precisely because the code runs fine and returns a plausible-looking number.

assessments.prompt: Which of these is the precise definition of a p-value for an observed test statistic?
options: The probability that H0 is true, given the observed data.
The probability, assuming H0 is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed.
The probability of making a Type I error on this specific test result.
The probability that the alternative hypothesis H1 is false.
assessments.explanation: This is the precise, conditional definition: a probability computed under the assumption that H0 holds, describing how likely data this extreme (or more) would be from sampling noise alone. Option A reverses the conditioning -- it describes P(H0 true | data), a different, generally unequal quantity that requires Bayesian reasoning to compute. Option C confuses a per-result probability with alpha, a long-run property of the testing procedure. Option D is effectively a restatement of option A's error, just phrased in terms of H1 instead of H0.

assessments.prompt: A model comparison yields p = 0.02. Which statement correctly describes what that number means?
options: If model A and model B truly had identical performance, a difference at least this large would arise from sampling noise alone only about 2% of the time.
There is a 2% chance the two models actually perform identically.
There is a 98% chance model B is genuinely better than model A.
2% of all hypothesis tests like this one turn out to be wrong.
assessments.explanation: This correctly keeps the conditioning direction intact: the 2% is the probability of the data, assuming H0 is true -- not a probability attached to H0 or H1 themselves. Options B and C both invert the conditional into a statement about how likely the hypotheses are, which a p-value does not and cannot establish on its own without a prior. Option D vaguely gestures at a Type I error rate but misstates it as a property of 'tests like this one turning out wrong' rather than the specific, conditional long-run false-positive rate that alpha (not directly the p-value) actually describes.

assessments.prompt: For a fixed alpha, how does the p-value comparison ('is p < alpha?') relate to the rejection-region comparison ('does the test statistic fall inside the region defined by alpha?')?
options: They can disagree, because they use fundamentally different mathematical criteria.
p < alpha holds exactly when the test statistic falls inside the rejection region defined by that same alpha -- they are the same decision, expressed two different ways.
Rejection regions are a fallback only usable when a p-value cannot be computed.
p-values only apply to two-sided tests, and rejection regions only apply to one-sided tests.
assessments.explanation: Because a p-value is a strictly decreasing function of how extreme the observed test statistic is, p < alpha and 'statistic inside the rejection region defined by alpha' are logically equivalent statements about the same underlying comparison -- a fact demonstrated directly in this concept across 1500 simulated datasets with zero mismatches. Option A contradicts this mathematical equivalence. Option C and option D both invent artificial restrictions; both approaches apply equally to one-sided and two-sided tests, and neither is a fallback for the other.

assessments.prompt: A colleague says: 'We got p = 0.04 comparing our new ranking model to the old one, so there's a 96% chance the new model is actually better.' Explain precisely what's wrong with this statement, and state what p = 0.04 actually tells you.
assessments.modelAnswer:
The statement confuses two different conditional probabilities that only look similar in casual English. A p-value of 0.04 is P(observing a difference at least this large | the new and old models truly perform identically) -- a probability computed entirely under the assumption that H0 is true, describing how surprising this data would be if there really were no difference. The colleague's claim, 'a 96% chance the new model is actually better,' is really asserting something close to P(H1 true | this data) -- the reverse conditional, and a fundamentally different quantity. Frequentist p-values never compute this reversed probability at all; doing so honestly requires Bayes' theorem and a prior probability that the new model is better before seeing any data, information a p-value calculation simply never uses. This is the same logical error as concluding, from a diagnostic test's known accuracy on people who have a disease, what fraction of positive-testing people 'actually have it' -- that answer depends heavily on how common the disease is to begin with, exactly the kind of prior information missing here.

What p = 0.04 genuinely tells you: if the new and old ranking models truly performed identically, data producing a gap this large or larger would arise from ordinary sampling noise only about 4% of the time. That's meaningful evidence against 'no real difference,' but it says nothing directly about how probable it is that H0 is true, nothing about how large or practically important the real improvement is, and nothing about the probability this specific result is a false positive -- alpha describes the test procedure's long-run error rate, not this one dataset's odds of being wrong.

concepts.title: Multiple Testing Corrections: Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR
concepts.description: Running many hypothesis tests against the same data inflates the overall chance of at least one false positive far above any single test's alpha, and Bonferroni (controlling the family-wise error rate) and Benjamini-Hochberg (controlling the false discovery rate) are two different, principled corrections, each suited to different ML experimentation scenarios.
learningObjectives: Explain the multiple comparisons problem: why running m independent tests, each at level alpha, inflates the probability of at least one false positive well above alpha.
Derive and compute the family-wise error rate (FWER) for m independent tests as 1 - (1 - alpha)^m, and show how quickly it grows with m.
Apply the Bonferroni correction (testing each hypothesis at alpha/m) and explain both why it controls FWER and why it becomes conservative as m grows.
Apply the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR), and explain how FDR differs conceptually from FWER.

Connect the multiple-testing problem explicitly to comparing many ML model or hyperparameter variants against a single validation set, and identify why this risk is easy to miss in iterative experimentation.

sections.heading: The Multiple Comparisons Problem
sections.body:
Every hypothesis test run at significance level alpha carries, by construction, an alpha probability of a false positive if H0 happens to be true for that particular test. That's a manageable, well-understood risk for a single, pre-planned test. It stops being manageable the moment you run many tests and ask whether *any* of them came back significant, because the probability that *at least one* false positive shows up across m independent tests, each individually at level alpha, assuming H0 is true for all of them, is:

```python
alpha = 0.05
for m in [1, 5, 20, 100]:
    fwer = 1 - (1 - alpha) ** m
    print(f"m={m}: {fwer:.4f}")
# m=1:   0.0500
# m=5:   0.2262
# m=20:  0.6415
# m=100: 0.9941
```

With just 20 independent tests, each individually using the seemingly cautious alpha=0.05, there's already about a 64% chance at least one comes back 'significant' by pure chance, even if nothing real is going on anywhere. At 100 tests, it's over 99% -- essentially guaranteed. This is the **multiple comparisons problem**, and it is directly, uncomfortably relevant to a routine ML workflow: evaluating 20 different hyperparameter configurations against a shared validation set, checking each one's improvement over a baseline with a naive per-test alpha=0.05 threshold, and picking whichever one 'won.' Even if none of the 20 configurations is genuinely any better than the baseline, there's roughly a 64% chance at least one of them clears the naive significance bar purely from validation-set noise -- and the natural instinct to report and ship whichever config happened to look best is exactly how that noise gets mistaken for a real result. This is the technical mechanism behind the informally-named **'garden of forking paths'** problem: the danger isn't any single test being computed wrong, it's that trying many paths and reporting only the one that looked good silently reintroduces the exact false-positive risk each individual alpha was supposed to keep small.

sections.heading: Controlling the Family-Wise Error Rate: Bonferroni
sections.body:
The **family-wise error rate (FWER)** is exactly the quantity from the previous section: the probability of at least one false positive anywhere across the whole family of m tests. The **Bonferroni correction** controls FWER with a strikingly simple rule: instead of rejecting each hypothesis at the original alpha, reject hypothesis i only if p_i < alpha / m.

```python
import numpy as np

p_values = np.array([0.001, 0.004, 0.009, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045,
                      0.070, 0.090, 0.150, 0.200, 0.280, 0.350, 0.450, 0.600, 0.800])
m = len(p_values)
alpha = 0.05

naive_reject = p_values < alpha
bonferroni_alpha = alpha / m
bonferroni_reject = p_values < bonferroni_alpha

print(f"naive (uncorrected) rejects: {naive_reject.sum()}")    # 6
print(f"Bonferroni-corrected alpha: {bonferroni_alpha:.5f}")   # 0.00333
print(f"Bonferroni rejects: {bonferroni_reject.sum()}")         # 1
```

Why does dividing by m guarantee FWER stays at or below alpha? By the union bound: the probability that *at least one* of m tests is a false positive is at most the *sum* of each individual test's false-positive probability. If every test is individually held to alpha/m, that sum is at most m * (alpha/m) = alpha, regardless of whether the tests are independent or correlated with each other in some complicated way -- which is a genuine virtue of Bonferroni: it needs no assumption about how the tests relate to each other to give this guarantee.

That same simplicity is also Bonferroni's weakness. As m grows, alpha/m shrinks fast -- with 100 tests and alpha=0.05, each individual test needs p < 0.0005 to survive correction, an extremely strict bar. This is the alpha/beta tradeoff from two concepts ago playing out again, just now spread across an entire family of tests at once: driving FWER down hard, by construction, drives beta up for every individual test in the family, meaning real, genuine effects increasingly fail to survive correction as m grows large. Bonferroni is the right tool when a single false positive anywhere in the family would be seriously costly and there's no cheap way to double-check a 'winner' afterward -- but it pays for that safety with a real, sometimes severe, loss of power.

sections.heading: Controlling the False Discovery Rate: Benjamini-Hochberg
sections.body:
The **false discovery rate (FDR)** asks a deliberately different, less conservative question than FWER. Rather than bounding the probability of *any* false positive anywhere in the family, FDR bounds the *expected proportion* of false positives *among the tests you actually flagged as significant* -- roughly, E[false positives / total rejections]. Controlling FDR at level alpha means you're willing to tolerate some false positives, as long as they make up a controlled, small fraction of whatever set of 'discoveries' you end up reporting -- a genuinely more permissive, and often more appropriate, standard whenever you plan to treat your flagged results as a shortlist for further investigation rather than a final, individually-guaranteed verdict.

The **Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure** achieves this with a clean algorithm: sort the m p-values ascending, p_(1) <= p_(2) <= ... <= p_(m), find the *largest* rank k such that p_(k) <= (k/m) * alpha, and reject every hypothesis at rank 1 through k.

```python
import numpy as np

def benjamini_hochberg(p_values, alpha):
    m = len(p_values)
    order = np.argsort(p_values)
    sorted_p = p_values[order]
    thresholds = (np.arange(1, m + 1) / m) * alpha
    below = sorted_p <= thresholds
    k = 0 if not np.any(below) else np.max(np.where(below)[0]) + 1
    reject_sorted = np.zeros(m, dtype=bool)
    reject_sorted[:k] = True
    reject = np.zeros(m, dtype=bool)
    reject[order] = reject_sorted
    return reject, k

reject, k = benjamini_hochberg(p_values, alpha=0.05)
print(f"BH rejects: {reject.sum()}")   # 3 -- more than Bonferroni's 1, fewer than the naive 6
```

On this same p-value list, BH rejects 3 hypotheses -- strictly more than Bonferroni's single rejection, but strictly fewer than the naive, uncorrected 6. The reason BH can afford to reject more than Bonferroni while still controlling a meaningful error rate is exactly the definitional difference between FWER and FDR: BH isn't promising zero-tolerance for any false positive anywhere in the family, it's promising that, on average, at most a controlled fraction of whatever you end up calling 'significant' will turn out to be false positives -- a substantively weaker, more forgiving guarantee, in exchange for meaningfully more power to catch real effects mixed in among many tested hypotheses.

sections.heading: Applying This to Comparing Many Model or Hyperparameter Variants
sections.body:
Translate the p-value list directly into an ML scenario: fifteen hyperparameter configurations, each compared against a baseline model on the same validation set, each producing a p-value for 'is this configuration's validation metric genuinely different from the baseline's.' The naive approach -- flag anything with p < 0.05 -- calls 6 of the 15 configurations significant improvements. Bonferroni, correctly accounting for the fact that 15 comparisons were actually made, calls only 1 significant. Benjamini-Hochberg, controlling a different and more permissive error notion, calls 3 significant. None of these three numbers is 'the' right answer in some absolute sense -- which one to use depends on what happens next.

If a 'significant' configuration is going straight to production with no further validation, Bonferroni's conservatism is the responsible choice: a false positive there is expensive, and FWER's zero-tolerance-per-family guarantee directly protects against that cost. If, instead, the flagged configurations are a shortlist headed for a further, independent confirmatory check -- a fresh holdout set, a longer-running A/B test, a human review -- Benjamini-Hochberg's more permissive FDR standard is often the better fit: it's explicitly built for exactly this 'flag candidates for follow-up' use case, tolerating a controlled fraction of false leads in the shortlist rather than demanding certainty about every single one up front.

The deeper fix, underneath either correction, is architectural rather than purely statistical: whenever it's feasible, decide the comparison plan (which configurations, which metric, which correction) *before* looking at results, and reserve a genuinely fresh, never-yet-touched holdout set for a final confirmatory test on whichever configuration 'won' during exploration. Correction procedures repair the accounting after the fact; a pre-registered plan and an untouched final holdout set prevent the problem from being created in the first place -- and in an iterative ML research process where a validation set gets revisited dozens of times across weeks of experimentation, that untouched final check is often what actually stands between a real result and an expensive-to-discover illusion.

examples.title: How Fast the Family-Wise Error Rate Grows
examples.code:
import numpy as np

alpha = 0.05
for m in [1, 5, 20, 100]:
    print(f"m={m}: FWER = {1 - (1 - alpha) ** m:.4f}")

# Confirm by simulation: draw m p-values from Uniform(0,1) -- exactly what
# a correctly-computed p-value looks like whenever H0 is genuinely true --
# and check how often at least one clears the naive alpha threshold.
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
m, n_trials = 20, 20000
at_least_one = sum(
    np.any(rng.uniform(0, 1, size=m) < alpha) for _ in range(n_trials)
)
print(f"simulated FWER for m=20: {at_least_one / n_trials:.4f}")
# analytic: 0.6415, simulated: ~0.637 -- matches
examples.explanation: A p-value, when H0 is genuinely true, is uniformly distributed between 0 and 1 -- which is exactly why comparing it to alpha gives a false-positive rate of precisely alpha for a single test, and exactly the property this simulation exploits to check the FWER formula empirically: drawing m independent Uniform(0,1) values is mathematically identical to drawing m p-values from m independent, genuinely-null tests. The simulated rate, about 0.637, lands close to the analytic 0.6415, confirming the formula isn't just an abstract derivation -- it's exactly what happens in practice when 20 independent, individually-innocent-looking tests are all run against truly null data.

examples.title: Bonferroni: Simple, Safe, and Conservative
examples.code:
import numpy as np

# p-values from comparing 15 hyperparameter configurations against a baseline
p_values = np.array([0.001, 0.004, 0.009, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045,
                      0.070, 0.090, 0.150, 0.200, 0.280, 0.350, 0.450, 0.600, 0.800])
m = len(p_values)
alpha = 0.05

naive_reject = p_values < alpha
bonferroni_alpha = alpha / m
bonferroni_reject = p_values < bonferroni_alpha

print(f"naive rejects (p < 0.05):        {naive_reject.sum()}")           # 6
print(f"Bonferroni-corrected threshold:  {bonferroni_alpha:.5f}")          # 0.00333
print(f"Bonferroni rejects:              {bonferroni_reject.sum()}")       # 1
examples.explanation: Only the very first configuration, with p=0.001, survives the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of 0.00333 -- the other five configurations that looked 'significant' under the naive alpha=0.05 threshold (p=0.004 through p=0.045) all fail to survive once the test correctly accounts for the fact that 15 comparisons were actually run. This is Bonferroni's FWER guarantee in action: it would rather risk missing several genuinely-better configurations than risk calling even one truly-no-better configuration a winner, across the whole family of 15 tests.

examples.title: Benjamini-Hochberg: More Power, a Different Guarantee
examples.code:
import numpy as np

def benjamini_hochberg(p_values, alpha):
    m = len(p_values)
    order = np.argsort(p_values)
    sorted_p = p_values[order]
    thresholds = (np.arange(1, m + 1) / m) * alpha
    below = sorted_p <= thresholds
    k = 0 if not np.any(below) else np.max(np.where(below)[0]) + 1
    reject_sorted = np.zeros(m, dtype=bool)
    reject_sorted[:k] = True
    reject = np.zeros(m, dtype=bool)
    reject[order] = reject_sorted
    return reject, k, sorted_p, thresholds

p_values = np.array([0.001, 0.004, 0.009, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045,
                      0.070, 0.090, 0.150, 0.200, 0.280, 0.350, 0.450, 0.600, 0.800])

reject, k, sorted_p, thresholds = benjamini_hochberg(p_values, alpha=0.05)

for rank in range(len(p_values)):
    flag = "reject" if rank < k else "  -- "
    print(f"rank {rank + 1:2d}: p={sorted_p[rank]:.3f}  BH threshold={thresholds[rank]:.5f}  {flag}")

print()
print(f"total BH rejections: {reject.sum()} (Bonferroni gave 1, naive p<0.05 gave 6)")
# BH rejects ranks 1-3 (p = 0.001, 0.004, 0.009) -- 3 total
examples.explanation: The first three sorted p-values (0.001, 0.004, 0.009) each fall below their own rank-scaled BH threshold (0.00333, 0.00667, 0.01), while rank 4's p-value (0.025) exceeds its threshold (0.01333) and every rank after that fails too -- so BH settles on k=3. Notice rank 2's p-value, 0.004, is actually larger than Bonferroni's flat threshold of 0.00333 and would be rejected by Bonferroni too only by coincidence in other datasets, but here it clears BH's more generous, rank-scaled threshold of 0.00667 -- this is exactly the extra power BH buys by controlling a different, more permissive error notion than FWER.

misconceptions.description: As long as each individual test correctly uses alpha=0.05, the overall set of conclusions from running many such tests is also protected at the 5% error level.
misconceptions.clarification: Alpha=0.05 protects only a single, individually-run test against a false positive. Running many such tests and looking for any significant result inflates the probability of at least one false positive well above 5% -- to about 23% for 5 tests, 64% for 20 tests, and over 99% for 100 tests, all while H0 might be true everywhere and nothing real is actually happening. Protecting the whole family of conclusions requires an explicit correction, such as Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg, applied on top of the individual per-test alpha.

misconceptions.description: Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg are just two implementations of the same correction, so it doesn't matter much which one you use.
misconceptions.clarification: They control fundamentally different quantities: Bonferroni bounds the probability of even a single false positive anywhere in the family (FWER), while Benjamini-Hochberg bounds the expected proportion of false positives among whatever gets flagged as significant (FDR) -- a substantively weaker, more permissive guarantee. On identical data, Benjamini-Hochberg routinely flags more hypotheses as significant than Bonferroni does, precisely because it's answering a more forgiving question; which one is appropriate depends on whether a single false positive anywhere would be seriously costly (favoring Bonferroni) or whether the flagged results are a shortlist headed for further confirmatory checking anyway (favoring Benjamini-Hochberg).

What does this print, and what does that number represent?

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to apply a Bonferroni correction across all the hypothesis tests that were actually run, but a reviewer noticed it under-corrects in a way that lets at least one result through that shouldn't survive. Find the bug and fix it.
exercises.code:

    significant = [p for p in p_values if p < alpha]
    correction_factor = len(significant)     # number of tests that already looked significant
    corrected_alpha = alpha / correction_factor
    return [p < corrected_alpha for p in p_values]

p_values = [0.001, 0.004, 0.007, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8]
print(bonferroni_reject(p_values))
hints: The Bonferroni correction divides alpha by the TOTAL number of tests actually conducted, m -- what does `correction_factor` here actually count instead?
Using only the count of already-significant results as the divisor is circular: it uses the outcome of the very comparison you're trying to correct as an input to the correction itself.
Fix correction_factor to be len(p_values) -- the full number of hypotheses tested, whether or not they individually looked significant beforehand.
exercises.solutionCode:
def bonferroni_reject(p_values, alpha=0.05):
    correction_factor = len(p_values)   # ALL tests actually conducted, not just the 'winners'
    corrected_alpha = alpha / correction_factor
    return [p < corrected_alpha for p in p_values]

p_values = [0.001, 0.004, 0.007, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8]
print(bonferroni_reject(p_values))
exercises.solutionExplanation: The buggy version counts only the 6 p-values that already cleared the uncorrected alpha=0.05 (0.001, 0.004, 0.007, 0.025, 0.030, 0.045) and divides alpha by that count (6), giving a corrected threshold of 0.05/6 = 0.00833 -- which incorrectly lets p=0.007 through as 'significant.' The correct Bonferroni correction divides alpha by m, the total number of hypotheses actually tested (9 here, including the 3 that were never close to significant), giving a stricter threshold of 0.05/9 = 0.00556, under which p=0.007 correctly fails to survive. The bug is a subtle circularity: using the number of hypotheses that already looked significant as the correction factor means the correction gets weaker precisely when more false positives are present to correct for, defeating the entire purpose of the correction.

assessments.prompt: A researcher runs 20 independent hypothesis tests, each at alpha=0.05, and reports that a 64% chance existed of at least one false positive turning up even if H0 were true everywhere. What is this 64% figure called, and how is it computed?
options: The false discovery rate (FDR), computed as alpha times the number of tests.
The family-wise error rate (FWER), computed as 1 - (1 - alpha)^m for m independent tests.
The statistical power of the combined set of 20 tests.
The Bonferroni-corrected significance level for the family of 20 tests.
assessments.explanation: 1 - (1 - 0.05)^20 is approximately 0.6415, matching the family-wise error rate: the probability that at least one false positive appears anywhere across all 20 tests, assuming H0 holds for every one of them. Option A misnames the quantity and misstates its formula -- FDR is a different quantity entirely, and 'alpha times the number of tests' isn't even a valid probability once it exceeds 1. Option C confuses this false-positive-rate calculation with power, which is about correctly detecting real effects, not the chance of a spurious one. Option D describes the corrected alpha/m threshold used to control FWER, not the FWER value itself.

assessments.prompt: Why does the Bonferroni correction guarantee that the family-wise error rate stays at or below alpha, regardless of how the individual tests relate to each other?
options: Because it requires all m tests to be statistically independent, which mathematically forces FWER down to alpha.

Because, by the union bound, the probability of at least one false positive across m tests is at most the sum of each test's individual false-positive probability, and holding each test to alpha/m keeps that sum at or below alpha.
Because dividing by m always makes each individual test's p-value exactly equal to zero.
Because it re-runs each test m additional times and only rejects if all m repetitions agree.
assessments.explanation: The union bound is precisely why Bonferroni works without needing any assumption about independence or correlation between the tests: summing each test's at-most-alpha/m false-positive probability across m tests gives a total of at most alpha, an upper bound that holds no matter how the tests are related. Option A inverts the actual advantage of Bonferroni -- it specifically does NOT require independence. Option C is a fabricated, nonsensical mechanism. Option D describes a completely different procedure (repeated replication), not what Bonferroni does.

assessments.prompt: A team is screening 50 hyperparameter configurations and plans to send any 'significant' ones to a separate, independent confirmatory test on a fresh holdout set before shipping anything. Which multiple-testing correction is the better fit for this initial screening step, and why?
options: Bonferroni, because family-wise error rate control should always be used regardless of context.

Benjamini-Hochberg, because it controls the false discovery rate -- a more permissive guarantee appropriate for a shortlist that will undergo further independent confirmation, and it will flag more real candidates than Bonferroni's stricter FWER control would.
Neither correction is necessary, since the follow-up confirmatory test will catch any mistakes anyway.
Naive, uncorrected alpha=0.05 per test, because the follow-up step makes the multiple comparisons problem irrelevant.

assessments.prompt: An ML engineer trains 30 different model variants overnight, checks each one's validation accuracy against the current production model using a separate hypothesis test per variant, and reports the single variant with the smallest p-value as 'the significant winner, p=0.01.' Explain what's wrong with this reporting practice and how it should be corrected.
assessments.modelAnswer:
Running 30 separate hypothesis tests and reporting only the smallest resulting p-value silently reintroduces the multiple comparisons problem, even though each individual test, taken alone, looks perfectly valid at alpha=0.05. If none of the 30 variants were actually any better than the production model, the probability that at least one of the 30 individual tests would still produce a 'significant' result purely from validation-set noise is substantial -- with m=30 and alpha=0.05, the family-wise error rate is already well over 75%, meaning a spurious 'winner' is more likely than not even when nothing real is happening. Reporting the single smallest p-value out of 30 as if it were the only test ever run -- rather than the survivor of an implicit 30-way search -- overstates the evidence for that variant dramatically; the p=0.01 headline figure never accounted for the other 29 chances the procedure had to produce a false positive.

The fix is to apply an explicit multiple-testing correction across all 30 comparisons actually made, not just report the smallest raw p-value. If shipping the winning variant directly, with no further validation, Bonferroni (comparing each p-value to alpha/30) is the conservative, appropriate choice, since a false positive there is directly costly. If the plan is to shortlist a few promising variants for a further, independent confirmatory test on fresh, never-touched data, Benjamini-Hochberg's false discovery rate control is usually the better fit, tolerating a controlled fraction of false leads in a shortlist that will be checked again anyway. Either way, the correction has to account for all 30 tests that were actually run, not merely the one that happened to look best.
